QF.id: AIFM AIFs in India and Suitability_9

question.text: Mira Family Office has approached Pragati AIF Manager about allocating to a new Category III long-short equity fund. As the AIF Manager, your suitability assessment concludes the family office is an APPROPRIATE LP. Which of the following is the WEAKEST reason to support that conclusion?

answer.text: Family offices typically have high holding capacity and can absorb illiquidity over the fund tenure
Family offices generally have the ability and willingness to take risk commensurate with Cat III's leveraged/derivative strategies
Family offices usually have ticket-size capacity well above the INR 1 crore AIF minimum
Family offices are classified as Retail Investors under SEBI regulations and therefore enjoy enhanced investor protection in Cat III AIFs

explanation.text: The Logic: Option D is false. Family offices are NOT classified as retail investors — they are sophisticated, non-retail capital. AIFs in fact raise capital ONLY from non-retail investors (privately pooled from institutions/HNIs/family offices). Options A, B and C are all legitimate suitability factors per Section 6.4. The Trap: The 'enhanced investor protection' phrasing sounds plausible but inverts reality — AIFs are explicitly outside the retail-protection regime precisely because their investors are deemed sophisticated. Cross-Exam Context: X-A Investment Adviser exam tests the retail vs non-retail classification and associated suitability regime; XIX-C expects the Manager to articulate why the fund is suitable in the context of the non-retail regime. Manager's Pro-Tip: Always obtain a written investor representation from the family office confirming non-retail sophistication and risk acknowledgement — in case of dispute, this document is the first thing a SEBI adjudicating officer will ask for.
